title: Pseudo-coherent complexes of modules are closed under direct summands
statement: Let $R$ be a ring and $m$ an integer. Call a complex of $R$-modules $C^\bullet$ $m$-pseudo-coherent if there are a bounded complex $E^\bullet$ of finite free $R$-modules and a map of complexes $E^\bullet\to C^\bullet$ inducing isomorphisms $H^i(E^\bullet)\to H^i(C^\bullet)$ for $i>m$ and a surjection $H^m(E^\bullet)\to H^m(C^\bullet)$. If $K^\bullet$ and $L^\bullet$ are complexes of $R$-modules such that $K^\bullet\oplus L^\bullet$ is $m$-pseudo-coherent, then $K^\bullet$ and $L^\bullet$ are $m$-pseudo-coherent. Consequently, if $K^\bullet\oplus L^\bullet$ is quasi-isomorphic to a bounded-above complex of finite free $R$-modules, then so are $K^\bullet$ and $L^\bullet$.

source.place: Tag 064X (more-algebra-lemma-summands-pseudo-coherent); the last clause through Tag 064T (more-algebra-lemma-pseudo-coherent: pseudo-coherent iff m-pseudo-coherent for every m)

proof.text: Assume $K^\bullet\oplus L^\bullet$ is $m$-pseudo-coherent. Since a witness $E^\bullet$ is a bounded complex of projective modules, morphisms $E^\bullet\to C^\bullet$ in $D(R)$ are represented by maps of complexes (Stacks, Derived Categories, Tag 064B), so for a complex the definition of the statement agrees with the one in $D(R)$ of the triangle lemma, and it is invariant under isomorphism in $D(R)$. The witness has $H^i(E^\bullet)=0$ for $i$ large, so $H^i(K^\bullet\oplus L^\bullet)=0$ for $i$ large; as cohomology commutes with finite direct sums, $K^\bullet$ and $L^\bullet$ are bounded above. The triangle $(K^\bullet\oplus L^\bullet,\,K^\bullet\oplus L^\bullet,\,L^\bullet\oplus L^\bullet[1])$, with first map $\mathrm{id}\oplus 0$, is distinguished as the direct sum of the distinguished triangles $(K^\bullet,K^\bullet,0)$ and $(L^\bullet,L^\bullet,L^\bullet\oplus L^\bullet[1])$ (Stacks, Derived Categories, Tag 05QS). An $m$-pseudo-coherent object is $(m+1)$-pseudo-coherent, since the same witness works. So the first term is $(m+1)$-pseudo-coherent and the second $m$-pseudo-coherent, and the first clause of [lem-pc-ring-pseudo-coherent-distinguished-triangle] shows that $L^\bullet\oplus L^\bullet[1]$ is $m$-pseudo-coherent.

source.place: Tag 064X, proof of lemma-summands-pseudo-coherent through the direct-sum distinguished triangle

proof.text: If $E^\bullet\to C^\bullet$ witnesses that $C^\bullet$ is $m$-pseudo-coherent, then $E^\bullet[1]\to C^\bullet[1]$ induces on $H^i$ the map $H^{i+1}(E^\bullet)\to H^{i+1}(C^\bullet)$, an isomorphism for $i\geq m$; so $C^\bullet[1]$ is $m$-pseudo-coherent. By induction $L^\bullet[n]\oplus L^\bullet[n+1]$ is $m$-pseudo-coherent for every $n\geq 0$. As $L^\bullet$ is bounded above, choose $n\geq 0$ with $H^i(L^\bullet[n])=0$ for all $i\geq m$; then the zero complex with the zero map $0\to L^\bullet[n]$ is a witness (isomorphisms $0\to 0$ for $i>m$, and $0\to H^m(L^\bullet[n])=0$ is surjective), so $L^\bullet[n]$ is $m$-pseudo-coherent (Stacks, More on Algebra, Tag 064W, part (1)). For $k=n,n-1,\dots,1$ use the split distinguished triangle $(L^\bullet[k],\,L^\bullet[k]\oplus L^\bullet[k-1],\,L^\bullet[k-1])$ (Tag 05QS): if $L^\bullet[k]$ is $m$-pseudo-coherent, it is $(m+1)$-pseudo-coherent, and the middle term is $m$-pseudo-coherent by the shifted decomposition, so the first clause of [lem-pc-ring-pseudo-coherent-distinguished-triangle] makes $L^\bullet[k-1]$ $m$-pseudo-coherent. At $k=1$ this gives that $L^\bullet$ is $m$-pseudo-coherent.

source.place: Tag 064X, induction and backward descent in the proof of lemma-summands-pseudo-coherent

proof.text: Exchanging $K^\bullet$ and $L^\bullet$, also $K^\bullet$ is $m$-pseudo-coherent. If $K^\bullet\oplus L^\bullet$ is isomorphic in $D(R)$ to a bounded-above complex $Q^\bullet$ of finite free modules, then for each $m$ the stupid truncation $\sigma_{\geq m}Q^\bullet$ (the terms of degree $\geq m$) is bounded and finite free, and $\sigma_{\geq m}Q^\bullet\to Q^\bullet\cong K^\bullet\oplus L^\bullet$ induces isomorphisms on $H^i$ for $i>m$ and a surjection on $H^m$; so $K^\bullet\oplus L^\bullet$, hence $K^\bullet$ and $L^\bullet$, are $m$-pseudo-coherent for every $m$. Conversely, let $C^\bullet$ be $m$-pseudo-coherent for every $m$; the $0$-pseudo-coherent witness gives $b$ with $H^i(C^\bullet)=0$ for $i>b$. Construct finite free $F^i$ and a map $f\colon F^\bullet\to C^\bullet$ downward, starting with $F^i=0$ for $i>b$: at stage $n$, $F^\bullet=F^{\geq n}$ is finite free with $H^i(f)$ an isomorphism for $i>n$ and surjective for $i=n$. Then the cone $M$ of $f$ has $H^i(M)=0$ for $i\geq n$ by the long exact sequence, and as $F^{\geq n}$ is $(n-1)$-pseudo-coherent (identity witness) and $C^\bullet$ is $(n-1)$-pseudo-coherent, the first clause of [lem-pc-ring-pseudo-coherent-distinguished-triangle] makes $M$ $(n-1)$-pseudo-coherent. Hence $H^{n-1}(M)$ is a finite module: for a witness $E^\bullet\to M$, the bounded finite free complex $E^\bullet$ is exact in degrees $\geq n$, so splitting it off from the top shows $\ker(d_E^{n-1})$ is finite projective, and $H^{n-1}(E^\bullet)$, a quotient of it, surjects onto $H^{n-1}(M)$ (Stacks, More on Algebra, Tag 064S). By the long exact sequence $H^{n-1}(C^\bullet)\to H^{n-1}(M)\to H^n(F^\bullet)\to H^n(C^\bullet)$, choose a finite free $F^{n-1}$ mapping onto $H^{n-1}(M)$ and lift to degree-$(n-1)$ cocycles of the cone, i.e. maps $F^{n-1}\to C^{n-1}$ and $F^{n-1}\to F^n$ compatible with the differentials. Then $H^n(f)$ becomes an isomorphism and $H^{n-1}(f)$ surjective. Iterating gives a bounded-above finite free complex $F^\bullet$ with a quasi-isomorphism $F^\bullet\to C^\bullet$ (Stacks, More on Algebra, Tag 064U). Applied to $K^\bullet$ and $L^\bullet$ this proves the final clause.
